THE SPREAD OF PEOPLES · DEEP DIVE

Chinese Explorers, Envoys & Geographers: Zhang Qian to Zheng He and Xu Xiake

Far outside the European Age of Sail taught in Western schools, Chinese officials, soldiers, monks, merchants, and field geographers crossed Eurasia and the Indian Ocean for nearly 1,800 years—recording eyewitness ethnographies from Fergana, Baghdad, Red Sea Africa, Nalanda, Sri Lanka, Paris, Malindi, and the Yangtze headwaters.

Chronological survey of ten landmark Chinese travelers across land and sea from Han envoy Zhang Qian (138 BCE) through Ming hydrographer Xu Xiake (1640 CE).

1. Han Envoys Opening Eurasia: Zhang Qian (138 BCE) & Gan Ying at the Persian Gulf (97 CE)

Chinese state exploration began in earnest in 138 BCE when Emperor Wu of Han dispatched court officer Zhang Qian westward to forge an alliance with the displaced Yuezhi against the Xiongnu. Captured almost immediately and held ten years in the steppe—where he married and kept his imperial yak-tail tally—Zhang Qian escaped across the Tian Shan to Fergana (Dayuan), Sogdiana (Kangju), and the Bactrian Oxus markets (Daxia). Though the Yuezhi declined war, Zhang Qian shocked Han strategists by spotting Sichuan Qiong bamboo staves and Shu cloth already reaching northern India and Bactria via Assam–Burma, catalysing imperial missions to Fergana, Wusun, and Parthia. [4] [10]

In 97 CE, Eastern Han Protector-General Ban Chao sent envoy Gan Ying straight across Arsacid Parthia (*Anxi*) to the head of the Persian Gulf (*Tiaozhi* / Charax Spasinu) intending to sail around Arabia to Rome (*Daqin*). Parthian mariners discouraged him—warning of three-month to two-year seasonal monsoon round-trips that left sailors homesick—so Gan Ying turned back while filing the earliest Chinese institutional account of Mesopotamia and Rome’s paved post-roads and rotational consuls. [10]

2. Buddhist Scholar-Explorers: Faxian (399), Xuanzang (629) & Yijing (671)

Long before European medieval travelogues, Chinese Buddhist monks braved mountains, deserts, and storm-swept straits to verify Vinaya monastic discipline and Yogacara philosophy in Sanskrit originals. Setting out around age 65 in 399 CE, Faxian walked across the Taklamakan ("guided by bleached human bones"), climbed Pamir rope bridges, studied six years in Gupta India and two years at Anuradhapura (Sri Lanka), then survived a leaking 200-passenger merchant ship battered 90 days across the Java Sea back to Shandong (*Foguoji*). [3] [1]

Crossing despite an imperial travel ban in 629 CE, Xuanzang forged friendships from Turpan to the Western Turkic Khagan near Tokmak and Samarkand before spending over a decade studying at Nalanda Mahavihara, debating before Emperor Harsha at Kannauj, and returning in 645 CE with 657 Sanskrit texts and Emperor Taizong’s geographical encyclopedia *Da Tang Xiyu Ji*. A generation later (671–695 CE), Yijing pioneered the maritime Persian–Srivijaya monsoon lane via Sumatra, preserving biographies of 56 international pilgrim monks. [2] [1]

3. Tang & Mongol-Era Surprises: Du Huan in Africa (758) & Rabban Bar Sauma in Paris/Bordeaux (1287)

Captured at the 751 CE Battle of Talas, Tang soldier-scholar Du Huan lived a decade across the early Abbasid Caliphate (Iraq, Syria, and *Molin*—modern Eritrea/Red Sea Ethiopia), returning to Guangzhou by sea in 762 CE. His preserved *Jingxingji* extracts in *Tongdian* record eyewitness details of early Friday mosque worship, Baghdad bazaar crafts, named Tang silk weavers and painters in Iraq, and the earliest first-person Chinese ethnography of Africa. [8]

Five centuries later (1275–1288 CE), Beijing-born Ongud Nestorian Christian monk Rabban Bar Sauma traveled from Kublai Khan’s Khanbaliq across the Taklamakan to Ilkhanid Iran and then served as Ilkhan Arghun’s ambassador to Europe—watching Mount Etna erupt off Naples, debating theology with Roman cardinals, touring Paris’s Sainte-Chapelle with King Philip IV, and celebrating liturgy before King Edward I of England at Bordeaux. [9]

4. Ocean Mariners & Scientific Hydrography: Wang Dayuan, Zheng He & Xu Xiake

Before Ming imperial treasure fleets ever launched, Yuan private merchant-scholar Wang Dayuan sailed twice out of Quanzhou (1330–1339 CE) aboard commercial ocean junks reaching Southeast Asia, Sri Lanka, Bengal, Hormuz, Mecca, and East Africa, profiling nearly 100 ports in *Daoyi Zhilüe* (1349 CE). Starting in 1405 CE under Admiral Zheng He and bilingual chroniclers Ma Huan and Fei Xin, seven state voyages projected Ming maritime diplomacy to Galle (leaving the 1409 trilingual stone stele), Calicut, Hormuz, Aden, Mogadishu, and Malindi—famously bringing back an East African giraffe presented by Bengal in 1414. [11] [5] [6]

In a radically different style of empirical exploration, late Ming private scholar Xu Xiake spent 34 years (1607–1640 CE) walking across 16 Chinese provinces carrying notebooks and compasses—cataloging over 100 tropical karst caves and proving through field hydrography in northern Yunnan that the Jinsha River, not the shorter Min River asserted in ancient classics, formed the true source of the Yangtze. [7]
